title: Noam Chomsky
summary: Linguist who argued that language rests on an innate grammar faculty, and a long-standing sceptic that statistical models tell us anything about the mind. His work in the 1950s helped end behaviourism and start cognitive science.

title: Stanisław Lem
summary: Polish science fiction writer and philosopher of technology. 'Solaris' (1961) is about an alien mind humans cannot understand; 'Golem XIV' (1981) is a set of lectures given by a superhuman computer to humanity.

title: Solomonoff induction
summary: Inventor of algorithmic probability, a mathematically ideal (though uncomputable) theory of learning by preferring the shortest programs that explain the data. He attended the 1956 Dartmouth workshop and his ideas underlie later formal theories of universal intelligence.

title: Gaia hypothesis
summary: The proposal that life on Earth, together with its inorganic surroundings, forms a self-regulating system that keeps the planet's atmosphere and climate suitable for life. James Lovelock and Lynn Margulis proposed it in the 1970s.

title: Aaron Sloman
summary: Philosopher and AI researcher at the University of Birmingham. He argued that philosophy of mind should be done by designing working minds, and he proposed the CogAff scheme that sorts mental processes into reactive, deliberative and reflective layers.

title: Perceptual illusions
summary: A viral photograph of a dress that some people saw as white and gold and others as blue and black. The cause is not settled; one explanation is that their visual systems made different assumptions about the lighting.

title: Quantum computing
summary: Computers that use quantum superposition and entanglement to solve certain problems, such as factoring, far faster than any known classical method. Building them is hard because qubits lose their quantum states (decohere) unless they are well isolated from the environment.

title: Cyc
summary: A decades-long project to hand-code millions of common-sense facts and rules so that a machine could reason like a person. Doug Lenat started it in 1984; critics such as Pedro Domingos have called it a catastrophic failure.

title: Boltzmann machine
by: Geoffrey Hinton, Terrence Sejnowski, David Ackley
summary: A neural network in which units constrain each other and the whole network tends toward low-energy states consistent with the inputs. The restricted version (RBM) drops within-layer links to make training feasible and helped launch deep learning.

title: Rodney Brooks: subsumption architecture
summary: Brooks argued that intelligence should be grown from the bottom up in robots that act in the world, using layers of simple behaviours with no central world model. The Roomba descends from this work.

title: Cognitive architectures: Soar and ACT-R
by: Allen Newell, John Laird; John R. Anderson
summary: A research tradition that tries to build complete, testable models of a whole mind (perception, memory, motivation, language) rather than isolated modules. It goes under names like cognitive systems, AGI and BICA.

title: The Cognitive Structure of Emotions
by: Andrew Ortony, Gerald Clore, Allan Collins
summary: A widely used scheme that sorts emotions into types according to how a person appraises events, agents and objects. Many software agents and artificial characters use it to generate emotions.

facet: The Gödelian argument and The Emperor's New Mind
title: Penrose and Hameroff: quantum consciousness
summary: Penrose's bestseller arguing that minds do something no algorithm can: see the truth of statements that formal systems cannot prove. He concludes that brains exploit non-computable physics.

title: Crick and Koch: neural correlates of consciousness
summary: Neuroscientist who pioneered the search for neural correlates of consciousness with Francis Crick and later helped develop and champion integrated information theory (IIT).

title: Ian Witten: cognition as compression
summary: English-born computer scientist at the University of Waikato, New Zealand, who co-invented prediction-based text compression (PPM) and popularised arithmetic coding; the idea is that to compress data well you must predict it, which requires modelling its structure.

title: Jürgen Schmidhuber
summary: The idea that learning is data compression, that curiosity is the reward for finding better compressions, and that beauty is how compressible something already is to the observer.

title: Greg Egan
summary: Hard science fiction about minds that run as software: copies of people living in simulations, citizens who are programs, and what personal identity means when a mind can be copied.

title: Hypercomputation
summary: Hypothetical machines that compute more than a Turing machine, for example by using infinitely precise real numbers or by sending the result of an endless computation back in time.

title: Chris Fields
summary: Physicist at the Allen Discovery Center at Tufts University who applies quantum information theory to biology and cognition, often with Michael Levin and Karl Friston. He argues that generic physical systems can be regarded as observers exchanging information with their environment.

title: David Deutsch: constructor theory
summary: Deutsch proposes restating physics in terms of which transformations are possible and which are impossible, rather than initial conditions and laws of motion. He also holds that science advances by explanation, not prediction.

facet: GANs as a model of dreaming
title: Deep learning
summary: A GAN trains two networks against each other: a generator invents samples and a discriminator judges whether they look real. Ian Goodfellow introduced them in 2014; later GANs became a major method for synthesising photorealistic images.

title: Deep learning
summary: An openly released image-generation model whose weights fit in about four gigabytes yet can generate photo-realistic images from any text prompt.

title: Deep learning
summary: Co-author of AlexNet and co-founder of OpenAI, known for early conviction that scaling neural networks would lead to AGI. He left OpenAI in 2024 to found Safe Superintelligence.

title: John Vervaeke: relevance realization
summary: Toronto cognitive scientist known for the lecture series 'Awakening from the Meaning Crisis'. He argues that the core of intelligence is 'relevance realization', and that wisdom traditions (Neoplatonism, Buddhism) cultivate it through practices rather than beliefs.

title: Large language models
summary: Chatbot products that users talk to as friends or partners. Replika is marketed as an AI companion; Claude is Anthropic's assistant.

title: Chollet: On the Measure of Intelligence
by: François Chollet (On the Measure of Intelligence)
summary: Chollet defines intelligence as the efficiency of acquiring new skills, not the possession of skills, and argues that current models mostly interpolate between things they have seen.

title: Gary Marcus
summary: Cognitive scientist and a well-known critic of deep learning. He argues that neural networks cannot reason reliably without built-in symbolic structure and that scaling them up will not yield general intelligence.

title: Murray Shanahan
summary: Imperial College and DeepMind researcher, author of 'Embodiment and the Inner Life', who describes LLMs as role-players simulating characters. He warns against describing such systems in human terms like 'knows' or 'believes' without care.
